Two Pandemics

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Covid-19 has taught us all the ‘new normal’ and a resilience to cope. Tonight we hear the stories from families who experienced the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic, some similarities and how they surviv

Unique Selling Point:
As the world faces social distancing and isolation we go back in history and re-visit a pandemic of similar nature from 1918 - the Spanish flu. We listen to stories of families and their collective memories of how people coped at the time with the disease and their resilience to survive against all odds. A hundred years later, despite facing another pandemic of global proportion, families are learning to cope with the ‘new normal’ and are adapting to a new way of life which ultimately are giving them the tools to come out stronger.


Summary:
In the early part of 1918 a disease began to sweep around the planet - a lethal virus that infected a third of the world’s population and left upwards of 50 million dead. The ‘Spanish flu’ spread simultaneously in Europe, Asia and North America over a twelve-month period. The First World War, although not the direct cause of its outbreak, contributed to its rapid spread worldwide. It became known as the Spanish flu, only because wartime censorship in other countries meant Spain was the first place it received widespread press attention.

Soldiers, were particularly vulnerable to infection. As they were constantly moved between different theatres of war across the globe they spread the virus to many countries. South Africa was not spared. Soldiers came back by ship and docked in Durban and Cape Town; those infected spread the disease as they travelled by train to every corner of the country. In September and October of 1918 the Spanish Flu had killed between 300 000 and 350 000 people: most of them were young adults between 18 and 40.

History is about to repeat as we live through another pandemic of global proportion. With Covid-19 we have learnt to live in lockdown; in isolation and have grown accustomed to the word ‘social distancing’. We look back at 1918 and link the past and the present as we make sense of the human experience and how people learnt to cope and came out stronger.


Further information:
We look at the lives of three families and their collective memories of the Spanish flu and how they now have a better understanding of the pandemic as they live through Covid-19.

Prof Howard Phillips will give context to the history during the time of the 1918 Spanish Flu in South Africa; research virologist, Prof Ed Rybicki will give a perspective to the origin, cause and effect of the pathogen; and we share the human experience with our families who have a far better understanding now of what their loved ones went through more than 100 years ago.

Our first story is about Thelma Reardon, a little girl from Durban who contracted the Spanish Flu when she was only five years old. She lived with her parents and four siblings in their tiny home in Ballance road next to the railway line - the poorer part of town. Thelma’s father died of stomach complications but the hardest for the little girl was losing her mother at that tender age.

Her story is told by her grand daughter, Jo-Anne Stemmet, a nurse from Somerset West who knew her granny Thelma very well and loved her dearly. “I now understand what she must have gone through as a five year old living in a tiny space where she had to face her mother’s death at that young age,” says Jo-Anne. Thelma grew up with her grandparents but was soon put to work when her granny became senile. “She was simply robbed of a childhood, and that left its scars on a deeper level where she often later in life became quiet, but her strong spirit helped her to pull through and she was certainly a role model for us grand children on facing challenges head on,” says Jo-Anne.

Our second story is told through the memories of a hundred-year old woman by the name of Floris Jawyer, born in District Six in 1920. She has a clear collection of the Spanish Flu through her late husband who was a carpenter and in his early twenties during that time. “I remember him telling me how the dead were taken to the top end of Loop street where they were buried in wooden boxes,” he said. “And some years later when he went back there and opened the boxes he said some of them must have been alive when they were thrown into the box as there were scratch marks on the lids that indicated that they might have still been alive at the time of being buried,” says Floris.

My husband told me that many people here in District Six had the influenza and many died. Times were tough.“I don’t find being in isolation particularly bad, but I do miss my children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren and hope it will soon be over so they can come and visit”, says Floris. Floris is a fiesty woman and her positive outlook on life is admirable.

Our third case study is David Bass, a retired doctor from Newlands, who’s father, Louis, was 10 years old when the pandemic swept across the country. Louis was one of 13 children living with their polish parents in District Six. Despite the fact that they all had a mild bout of the influenza they all survived. In an audio recording of Louis’ memories of the Spanish flu he tells the story of how they ate oranges, took aspirin and lozenges and made chicken soup - a good old hearty broth to help fight off the symptoms. This is an extract from his audio recording from 2002 before he died.

“Then came the next disaster, a virulent germ - we call it the Spanish Flu spread over the world. It was a virulent disease: people went out in the morning and dropped dead in the streets in the afternoon. I saw it; I saw people lying in the streets in Chapel street, dead. And there was nobody, everybody was ill. The welfare was so busy; the bodies had to lay there till eventually some organisation came and picked them up.”

David Bass remembers his father as a strong willed and positive person and now has a better understanding of what his father and siblings experienced a little more than a hundred years ago during the outbreak of the pandemic.

Historian Prof Howard Phillips recorded that the working-class areas of Cape Town were hardest hit: District Six, Bo-Kaap, “Little Sicily” near the harbour, Woodstock, Salt River, the African locations at the docks and the local black township, Ndabeni. On 10 October 1918, 442 deaths were recorded in one day. Overall, the Cape Town death toll topped 4 300, or 3,5% of the population.

Phillips has published a collection of testimonies of survivors in his book “Memories of the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918” in which he includes 126 interviews and letters collected in the 1970s and has written several papers on the subject. Phillips will expand on the geographical spread, the target groups, the health systems that were in place (or lack thereof) and how it affected the different demographics of South Africa.

Prof Ed Rybicki is an expert biotechnologist and vaccinologist and works at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at UCT. He has extensive experience in molecular virology and virus diversity studies with plant and human and animal viruses, which has led to his working with a number of vaccine and expression system platforms. He will give a biomedical perspective of the deadly Spanish flu: the origin - aquatic birds and pig farms - the spread - to military camps during the war and the treatment - aspirin and quinine - none of which helped.

Treatment
The story is a historic drama told through the family members and their collective memories of loved ones lost; the long term effect it had on the generations left behind; the insight they have gained due to a similar situation they are experiencing with the Coronavirus, and their resilience in coping with Covid-19.

The history and biomedical facts gives the framework to understand the world we live in and link the past with the present.

Visuals: With our presenter now in Cape Town, interviews and links will be done on location. Archive material, memorabilia and artifacts will be used as additional material to paint the picture of the past.

Script:


Final Script: Two Pandemics
Date: 14 August 2020
Duration: 10 minutes

V/O A century ago an event swept through the globe that would change the course of history. A deadly virus claimed upwards of 50 million people tearing many families apart.

Up music

V/O As we experience the Covid-19 pandemic, stories of the Spanish flu re-emerge from the dusty pages of our collective memories. Jo Stemmetts’ granny Thelma, who lived in Durban, survived the flu but lost her mother.

UP sound: “She looked beautiful. Jo Stemmett: Ja definitely. She was an amazing woman.”

Jo Stemmett: Granddaughter of Thelma Reardon - My grandmother and I were very very close. One of the most important stories that she told me was when she was very, very small and she had the Spanish flu, and how she lost her mom in that epidemic and she was left orphaned at the age of 6.

V/O Susan Hayden’s grandfather, Richard Radford Hayden, was only eleven when he too became an orphan.

Susan Hayden: Granddaughter of Richard Radford Hayden: Families have narratives and the narrative in our family was always that grandpa had this terrible thing happen to him. His mom and dad were very ill and his grand dad and him were nursing them together with some neighbours and on a Sunday morning his mom died and the following Tuesday his dad died.

V/O As the influenza claimed the lives of parents, flu-orphans were left behind.

Up song:
“I had a little bird
And its name was Enza
I opened the window
And in-flew-Enza”

V/O As children skipped to the rhythm of the nursery rhyme soldiers fought on the battlefields in Europe. It was March 1918 and WW1 was coming to an end.

UP sound - Voice recording of Dr Louis Bass: “You know as you go along memories come back to you and these two events were shattering events: In 1914 started WW1. I remember it clearly. I was just 6 years old. Then came the next disaster, a virulent germ - we call it the Spanish Flu spread over the world. It was a virulent disease: people went out in the morning and dropped dead in the streets in the afternoon.”

Up sound

V/O Memories of the pandemic come in many different forms. David Bass from Newlands in Cape Town discovered a cassette recording of his late father after he passed away in 2002.

David Bass: Son of Dr Louis Bass: It was astonishing to me, particularly his description of the historic events such as his experiences during the First World War and the Spanish flu were quite astounding because firstly, the quality of his memory and secondly the detail.

Link: The 1918 influenza was nicknamed The Spanish flu. Only because there was no wartime censorship in Spain where it was first reported in the early stages of 1918. The news quickly spread. Here we have a local South African newspaper dated 10 October 1918 with the headline: “World in the grip of flu”.

V/O Howard Phillips, emeritus professor of history at the University of Cape Town, wrote in his book: “In a Time of Plague” some of the stories of Spanish flu survivors and their vivid account of what happened.

Prof Howard Phillips: Historian - “You would see someone in the morning and he or she would say, I don’t feel right. By that evening they were already in their graves.”

V/O Ed Rybicki, research virologist from the University of Cape Town has an interest in influenza and the origin of this particular strain of virus which became known as the Spanish flu.

Masa Kekana: Where did the Spanish flu originate?

Prof Ed Rybicki: Virologist - We don’t actually know absolutely. Very probably it came out of birds initially, possibly through another agent like a pig and then straight into humans.

Masa Kekana: How did it spread from animals to humans?

Prof Ed Rybicki: The military camps in France and Belgium at the time were huge and they had enormous populations of farm animals. So people who were infected in Europe because that is where the main melting pot was then got dispersed in 1918 when everybody went home again, get on a ship, take the virus with you.

V/O Like with Covid-19, the Spanish flu was transmitted to people through droplets and aerosols.

Prof Howard Phillips: Historian - The conditions of World War 1 was tailor made for the spread of an infectious disease - large numbers of young men clustered together, without a doubt the conditions of WW1 were of enormous importance in the speed with which it was spread across land, across sea.

V/O Ships arrived in Cape Town and Durban harbour bringing troops back home. Those who showed symptoms of the flu were hospitalised but with no treatments for influenza back in 1918 they were sent home to self-medicate and reduce the risk of infection to others.

Link: Businesses shut, schools closed and people isolating at home, sounds familiar? These are the exact scenes that took place during the 1918 Spanish flu outbreak. (pause - 8 frames)

Masa Kekana: And the people who were infected, what symptoms did they have?

Prof Ed Rybicki: The first symptoms that people noticed apart from the standard sniffle and cough were the fact that people’s lips were turning blue because their lungs were so badly affected and fluid was accumulating so fast that they were actually not getting oxygen.

V/O Unlike Covid-19, the Spanish flu attacked young and healthy adults.

Prof Ed Rybicki: The age group is most badly affected which is say between 25 and 35 had not had prior exposure to a virus like this before whereas people older than that had. So there were two big epidemics in 1880’s. People born round about that time would be protected if it looked anything like the 1918 virus.

V/O It was the end of the war and soldiers were free to return home by train. They passed through towns, cities and the mines where the virus spread rapidly. Many young miners in the diamond mines in Kimberley and gold mines in the Witwatersrand fled from the death traps to get home where they carried it to more isolated and remote parts of the country. In October 1918 it reached its peak.

Prof Howard Phillips: Contemporaries call it black October, where the epidemic rampage through a country killing 5, 6 percent of the population in 5 or 6 weeks. It is an utter calamity. 350 000 South Africans died.

Link: Many buildings across the country were turned into make-shift hospitals. The city hall here in Cape Town was one of the temporary centres where people queued for food and medicine.

Prof Howard Philips: There were soup kitchens, there were town halls, churches where lemons were made available. They thought vitamin C might help. So it was really trying to curb this unfolding disaster.

David Bass: My father speaks about having nothing to counter the flu. They ate oranges and they took throat lozenges and they had aspirin and nothing else.

Prof Howard Phillips: I interviewed a man whose father was a GP in CT in 1918. And he went around with his dad on his rounds and he said to me: “what sticks in my memory most is that it was the first time I ever saw my dad cry. He was crying for his inability to do anything for the patients who were dying left, right and center”.

V/O Today there are few survivors of the Spanish flu. Jawyer Floris turned 100 years old on the 1st of May this year. She lives in District Six where she was born. She clearly remembers an anecdote from her late husband who was a young carpenter in the area.

Masa Kekana: Mrs Floris what did your husband tell you about the Spanish flu?

Jawyer Floris: He used to tell me that they had the wagons with the little lantern going from house to house, and then they would come and pick up the bodies, 34 bodies sometimes at a time and they would take it to the top of Longmarket street and there they buried it. One household they take 3 to 4 bodies away a day from just one house.

V/O On the kist next to the chair where she sits are the photographs of her many children, grandchildren and great grandchildren. Covid-19 has had its challenges, especially for her.

Masa Kekana: Are you missing your grandchildren and great grandchildren?

Floris Jawyer: Yes I really miss them. We are longing to see them running in and out like they usually did.

Up sound - make this up sound longer

Jo Stemmett: I look at the pandemic now and the effect it had on our lives. I look back and it is just such a stark contrast to what it was then.

V/O Jo remembers her granny as a very affectionate person who at an early age left school to look after her grandparents who raised her.

Jo Stemmett: She used to get quite upset if you did not give her the level of affection she wanted. It was probably a strong sense of abandonment she had and of loss.

V/O Susan recalls her grandfather sitting at the kitchen table unable to engage with the family and show affection to his children.

Susan Hayden: I think a lot of who he was was the result of tremendous trauma that he suffered as a child... I think he never really got over that.

V/O Susan contracted Covid-19 in March and went through a low period of uncertainty of what the future held for her and her family, and for the first time since her grandfather died, she felt a sense of kinship with him.

Masa Kekana: Having the memories of what your grandfather went through with the Spanish flu, did it feel like it came full circle?

Susan Hayden: It did a little bit. We have technology and we have science, so suddenly a hundred years later to be in exactly the same situation was very surreal.

Up sound

Masa Kekana: With what is happening right now what do you think of this coronavirus?

Floris Jawyer: I didn't put much thought to it. It is one of the things that had to happen and it has got a beginning and definitely it has got an end. It must end.

___________________________________________________________________________

In 1918 a deadly virus swept across the planet casting a shadow of death over 50 million people. Locked in our pandemic 102 years later we share the stories of Spanish flu survivors.

Promo 2
Up song: “I had a little bird, his name was Enza,….(continue song under the voice)
V/O 50 Million people died of the 1918 Spanish influenza leaving many flu-orphans behind.
Up song….

Over 350 000 people died in South Africa from the 1918 Spanish flu; It took the lives of the young and healthy leaving orphans behind. We bring you their stories.

A deadly virus claimed upwards of 50 million people tearing many families apart. Up music V/O As we experience the Covid-19 pandemic, stories of the Spanish flu re-emerge from the dusty pages of our collective memories. Jo Stemmetts’ granny Thelma, who lived in Durban, survived the flu but lost her mother. UP sound: “She looked beautiful. Jo Stemmett: Ja definitely. She was an amazing woman.” Jo Stemmett: Granddaughter of Thelma Reardon - My grandmother and I were very very close. One of the most important stories that she told me was when she was very, very small and she had the Spanish flu, and how she lost her mom in that epidemic and she was left orphaned at the age of 6. V/O Susan Hayden’s grandfather, Richard Radford Hayden, was only eleven when he too became an orphan. Susan Hayden: Granddaughter of Richard Radford Hayden: Families have narratives and the narrative in our family was always that grandpa had this terrible thing happen to him. His mom and dad were very ill and his grand dad and him were nursing them together with some neighbours and on a Sunday morning his mom died and the following Tuesday his dad died. V/O As the influenza claimed the lives of parents, flu-orphans were left behind. Up song: “I had a little bird And its name was Enza I opened the window And in-flew-Enza” V/O As children skipped to the rhythm of the nursery rhyme soldiers fought on the battlefields in Europe. It was March 1918 and WW1 was coming to an end. UP sound - Voice recording of Dr Louis Bass: “You know as you go along memories come back to you and these two events were shattering events: In 1914 started WW1. I remember it clearly. I was just 6 years old. Then came the next disaster, a virulent germ - we call it the Spanish Flu spread over the world. It was a virulent disease: people went out in the morning and dropped dead in the streets in the afternoon.” Up sound V/O Memories of the pandemic come in many different forms. David Bass from Newlands in Cape Town discovered a cassette recording of his late father after he passed away in 2002. David Bass: Son of Dr Louis Bass: It was astonishing to me, particularly his description of the historic events such as his experiences during the First World War and the Spanish flu were quite astounding because firstly, the quality of his memory and secondly the detail. Link: The 1918 influenza was nicknamed The Spanish flu. Only because there was no wartime censorship in Spain where it was first reported in the early stages of 1918. The news quickly spread. Here we have a local South African newspaper dated 10 October 1918 with the headline: “World in the grip of flu”. V/O Howard Phillips, emeritus professor of history at the University of Cape Town, wrote in his book: “In a Time of Plague” some of the stories of Spanish flu survivors and their vivid account of what happened. Prof Howard Phillips: Historian - “You would see someone in the morning and he or she would say, I don’t feel right. By that evening they were already in their graves.” V/O Ed Rybicki, research virologist from the University of Cape Town has an interest in influenza and the origin of this particular strain of virus which became known as the Spanish flu. Masa Kekana: Where did the Spanish flu originate? Prof Ed Rybicki: Virologist - We don’t actually know absolutely. Very probably it came out of birds initially, possibly through another agent like a pig and then straight into humans. Masa Kekana: How did it spread from animals to humans? Prof Ed Rybicki: The military camps in France and Belgium at the time were huge and they had enormous populations of farm animals. So people who were infected in Europe because that is where the main melting pot was then got dispersed in 1918 when everybody went home again, get on a ship, take the virus with you. V/O Like with Covid-19, the Spanish flu was transmitted to people through droplets and aerosols. Prof Howard Phillips: Historian - The conditions of World War 1 was tailor made for the spread of an infectious disease - large numbers of young men clustered together, without a doubt the conditions of WW1 were of enormous importance in the speed with which it was spread across land, across sea. V/O Ships arrived in Cape Town and Durban harbour bringing troops back home. Those who showed symptoms of the flu were hospitalised but with no treatments for influenza back in 1918 they were sent home to self-medicate and reduce the risk of infection to others. Link: Businesses shut, schools closed and people isolating at home, sounds familiar? These are the exact scenes that took place during the 1918 Spanish flu outbreak. (pause - 8 frames) Masa Kekana: And the people who were infected, what symptoms did they have? Prof Ed Rybicki: The first symptoms that people noticed apart from the standard sniffle and cough were the fact that people’s lips were turning blue because their lungs were so badly affected and fluid was accumulating so fast that they were actually not getting oxygen. V/O Unlike Covid-19, the Spanish flu attacked young and healthy adults. Prof Ed Rybicki: The age group is most badly affected which is say between 25 and 35 had not had prior exposure to a virus like this before whereas people older than that had. So there were two big epidemics in 1880’s. People born round about that time would be protected if it looked anything like the 1918 virus. V/O It was the end of the war and soldiers were free to return home by train. They passed through towns, cities and the mines where the virus spread rapidly. Many young miners in the diamond mines in Kimberley and gold mines in the Witwatersrand fled from the death traps to get home where they carried it to more isolated and remote parts of the country. In October 1918 it reached its peak. Prof Howard Phillips: Contemporaries call it black October, where the epidemic rampage through a country killing 5, 6 percent of the population in 5 or 6 weeks. It is an utter calamity. 350 000 South Africans died. Link: Many buildings across the country were turned into make-shift hospitals. The city hall here in Cape Town was one of the temporary centres where people queued for food and medicine. Prof Howard Philips: There were soup kitchens, there were town halls, churches where lemons were made available. They thought vitamin C might help. So it was really trying to curb this unfolding disaster. David Bass: My father speaks about having nothing to counter the flu. They ate oranges and they took throat lozenges and they had aspirin and nothing else. Prof Howard Phillips: I interviewed a man whose father was a GP in CT in 1918. And he went around with his dad on his rounds and he said to me: “what sticks in my memory most is that it was the first time I ever saw my dad cry. He was crying for his inability to do anything for the patients who were dying left, right and center”. V/O Today there are few survivors of the Spanish flu. Jawyer Floris turned 100 years old on the 1st of May this year. She lives in District Six where she was born. She clearly remembers an anecdote from her late husband who was a young carpenter in the area. Masa Kekana: Mrs Floris what did your husband tell you about the Spanish flu? Jawyer Floris: He used to tell me that they had the wagons with the little lantern going from house to house, and then they would come and pick up the bodies, 34 bodies sometimes at a time and they would take it to the top of Longmarket street and there they buried it. One household they take 3 to 4 bodies away a day from just one house. V/O On the kist next to the chair where she sits are the photographs of her many children, grandchildren and great grandchildren. Covid-19 has had its challenges, especially for her. Masa Kekana: Are you missing your grandchildren and great grandchildren? Floris Jawyer: Yes I really miss them. We are longing to see them running in and out like they usually did. Up sound - make this up sound longer Jo Stemmett: I look at the pandemic now and the effect it had on our lives. I look back and it is just such a stark contrast to what it was then. V/O Jo remembers her granny as a very affectionate person who at an early age left school to look after her grandparents who raised her. Jo Stemmett: She used to get quite upset if you did not give her the level of affection she wanted. It was probably a strong sense of abandonment she had and of loss. V/O Susan recalls her grandfather sitting at the kitchen table unable to engage with the family and show affection to his children. Susan Hayden: I think a lot of who he was was the result of tremendous trauma that he suffered as a child... I think he never really got over that. V/O Susan contracted Covid-19 in March and went through a low period of uncertainty of what the future held for her and her family, and for the first time since her grandfather died, she felt a sense of kinship with him. Masa Kekana: Having the memories of what your grandfather went through with the Spanish flu, did it feel like it came full circle? Susan Hayden: It did a little bit. We have technology and we have science, so suddenly a hundred years later to be in exactly the same situation was very surreal. Up sound Masa Kekana: With what is happening right now what do you think of this coronavirus? Floris Jawyer: I didn't put much thought to it. It is one of the things that had to happen and it has got a beginning and definitely it has got an end. It must end. ___________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1 In 1918 a deadly virus swept across the planet casting a shadow of death over 50 million people. Locked in our pandemic 102 years later we share the stories of Spanish flu survivors. Promo 2 Up song: “I had a little bird, his name was Enza,….(continue song under the voice) V/O 50 Million people died of the 1918 Spanish influenza leaving many flu-orphans behind. Up song…. Promo 3 Over 350 000 people died in South Africa from the 1918 Spanish flu; It took the lives of the young and healthy leaving orphans behind. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Covid-19 has taught us all the ‘new normal’ and a resilience to cope. Tonight we hear the stories from families who experienced the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic, some similarities and how they surviv
metadata.Unique Selling Point: As the world faces social distancing and isolation we go back in history and re-visit a pandemic of similar nature from 1918 - the Spanish flu. We listen to stories of families and their collective memories of how people coped at the time with the disease and their resilience to survive against all odds. A hundred years later, despite facing another pandemic of global proportion, families are learning to cope with the ‘new normal’ and are adapting to a new way of life which ultimately are giving them the tools to come out stronger.
metadata.Summary: In the early part of 1918 a disease began to sweep around the planet - a lethal virus that infected a third of the world’s population and left upwards of 50 million dead. The ‘Spanish flu’ spread simultaneously in Europe, Asia and North America over a twelve-month period. The First World War, although not the direct cause of its outbreak, contributed to its rapid spread worldwide. It became known as the Spanish flu, only because wartime censorship in other countries meant Spain was the first place it received widespread press attention. Soldiers, were particularly vulnerable to infection. As they were constantly moved between different theatres of war across the globe they spread the virus to many countries. South Africa was not spared. Soldiers came back by ship and docked in Durban and Cape Town; those infected spread the disease as they travelled by train to every corner of the country. In September and October of 1918 the Spanish Flu had killed between 300 000 and 350 000 people: most of them were young adults between 18 and 40. History is about to repeat as we live through another pandemic of global proportion. With Covid-19 we have learnt to live in lockdown; in isolation and have grown accustomed to the word ‘social distancing’. We look back at 1918 and link the past and the present as we make sense of the human experience and how people learnt to cope and came out stronger.
metadata.Further information: We look at the lives of three families and their collective memories of the Spanish flu and how they now have a better understanding of the pandemic as they live through Covid-19. Prof Howard Phillips will give context to the history during the time of the 1918 Spanish Flu in South Africa; research virologist, Prof Ed Rybicki will give a perspective to the origin, cause and effect of the pathogen; and we share the human experience with our families who have a far better understanding now of what their loved ones went through more than 100 years ago. Our first story is about Thelma Reardon, a little girl from Durban who contracted the Spanish Flu when she was only five years old. She lived with her parents and four siblings in their tiny home in Ballance road next to the railway line - the poorer part of town. Thelma’s father died of stomach complications but the hardest for the little girl was losing her mother at that tender age. Her story is told by her grand daughter, Jo-Anne Stemmet, a nurse from Somerset West who knew her granny Thelma very well and loved her dearly. “I now understand what she must have gone through as a five year old living in a tiny space where she had to face her mother’s death at that young age,” says Jo-Anne. Thelma grew up with her grandparents but was soon put to work when her granny became senile. “She was simply robbed of a childhood, and that left its scars on a deeper level where she often later in life became quiet, but her strong spirit helped her to pull through and she was certainly a role model for us grand children on facing challenges head on,” says Jo-Anne. Our second story is told through the memories of a hundred-year old woman by the name of Floris Jawyer, born in District Six in 1920. She has a clear collection of the Spanish Flu through her late husband who was a carpenter and in his early twenties during that time. “I remember him telling me how the dead were taken to the top end of Loop street where they were buried in wooden boxes,” he said. “And some years later when he went back there and opened the boxes he said some of them must have been alive when they were thrown into the box as there were scratch marks on the lids that indicated that they might have still been alive at the time of being buried,” says Floris. My husband told me that many people here in District Six had the influenza and many died. Times were tough.“I don’t find being in isolation particularly bad, but I do miss my children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren and hope it will soon be over so they can come and visit”, says Floris. Floris is a fiesty woman and her positive outlook on life is admirable. Our third case study is David Bass, a retired doctor from Newlands, who’s father, Louis, was 10 years old when the pandemic swept across the country. Louis was one of 13 children living with their polish parents in District Six. Despite the fact that they all had a mild bout of the influenza they all survived. In an audio recording of Louis’ memories of the Spanish flu he tells the story of how they ate oranges, took aspirin and lozenges and made chicken soup - a good old hearty broth to help fight off the symptoms. This is an extract from his audio recording from 2002 before he died. “Then came the next disaster, a virulent germ - we call it the Spanish Flu spread over the world. It was a virulent disease: people went out in the morning and dropped dead in the streets in the afternoon. I saw it; I saw people lying in the streets in Chapel street, dead. And there was nobody, everybody was ill. The welfare was so busy; the bodies had to lay there till eventually some organisation came and picked them up.” David Bass remembers his father as a strong willed and positive person and now has a better understanding of what his father and siblings experienced a little more than a hundred years ago during the outbreak of the pandemic. Historian Prof Howard Phillips recorded that the working-class areas of Cape Town were hardest hit: District Six, Bo-Kaap, “Little Sicily” near the harbour, Woodstock, Salt River, the African locations at the docks and the local black township, Ndabeni. On 10 October 1918, 442 deaths were recorded in one day. Overall, the Cape Town death toll topped 4 300, or 3,5% of the population. Phillips has published a collection of testimonies of survivors in his book “Memories of the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918” in which he includes 126 interviews and letters collected in the 1970s and has written several papers on the subject. Phillips will expand on the geographical spread, the target groups, the health systems that were in place (or lack thereof) and how it affected the different demographics of South Africa. Prof Ed Rybicki is an expert biotechnologist and vaccinologist and works at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at UCT. He has extensive experience in molecular virology and virus diversity studies with plant and human and animal viruses, which has led to his working with a number of vaccine and expression system platforms. He will give a biomedical perspective of the deadly Spanish flu: the origin - aquatic birds and pig farms - the spread - to military camps during the war and the treatment - aspirin and quinine - none of which helped. Treatment The story is a historic drama told through the family members and their collective memories of loved ones lost; the long term effect it had on the generations left behind; the insight they have gained due to a similar situation they are experiencing with the Coronavirus, and their resilience in coping with Covid-19. The history and biomedical facts gives the framework to understand the world we live in and link the past with the present. Visuals: With our presenter now in Cape Town, interviews and links will be done on location. Archive material, memorabilia and artifacts will be used as additional material to paint the picture of the past.
